title: The Quiet Road
subtitle: Twenty-One Days with The Imitation of Christ for the Pilgrim
description_short: Twenty-one days with a 600-year-old classic of the inner life: a morning reading and an evening reflection for each day on the Camino Francés. Slow, honest and quiet.
description_long:
The Imitation of Christ was written in Latin in the 1420s and is traditionally attributed to Thomas à Kempis, a canon regular who lived most of his life in a small community near Zwolle. It has been read, copied and translated for six centuries, and it is a book about the things a long walk brings to the surface: tiredness, doubt, the wish to begin again, the people we walk beside, and what we are really looking for.

The Quiet Road is made to go with the Camino Francés. It has twenty-one days, three weeks, one for each day of walking or each day at home. Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three. The morning begins with a short passage from the classic, quoted word for word from William Benham's translation, which is in the public domain. Then comes a reflection that starts from something on the road: an early start, a blister, a bench, a stranger's kindness. Then two small things to carry for the next hour, a question and a practice that needs nothing but attention. The evening looks back over the day with two or three gentle questions and ends with a short original prayer, open enough to be said as a wish by a reader who prays differently, or who does not pray.

The days follow an arc from setting out, through the middle of the road, to arrival and return. The classic is a Christian book and this book says so plainly. It invites and does not push, and it is honest where Thomas is hard to follow. Read it on a bench, in a pilgrim hostel bunk, or at your own kitchen table once the walking is done.
